This page goes with **Chapter 30, Introduction to Counterpoint** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/IntroductionToCounterpoint.html). Read each section there first. It builds on [Voice Leading Triads](voice-leading-triads.qmd) (the types of motion and the rules of melody in 26.1 and 26.4).

**How the page works.** Each example is drawn on a grand staff, plays when you press **Play**, and is **marked by the same checker** that marks your exercises: a green *Right*
passes it, a red *Wrong* shows what the checker says. In the exercises the given notes are greyed; type the others (`E4`, `F#4`, `Bb3`; **Up** and **Down** move a step in the key,
**Shift** a half step) and press **Check**.

Every counterpoint is written in **two voices** against a given **cantus firmus** (c.f.), a plain melody in whole notes. Here the cantus firmus is in the lower voice (counterpoint above) or in the upper voice (counterpoint below); the page says which.

## 30.1 Species counterpoint

Fux's *Gradus ad Parnassum* (1725) teaches writing by **species**: one, two, three or four notes against each whole note of the cantus firmus, in the style of Palestrina. Counterpoint is the sounding together of
melodic lines (a **contrapuntal** texture), in contrast to melody and accompaniment (**homophonic**). The book's rules are a simplified version of Fux's; the page's checker marks first and second species. Third, fourth and fifth species are described below but not checked.

## 30.2 First species: note against note

Write one whole note for each note of the cantus firmus. The rules (simplified from Fux, as in the book):

- **Begin and end on a unison or octave.** Approach the final octave by **contrary motion**: one voice 7 to 8 (a half step up, with a raised leading tone in G mixolydian, D dorian and A aeolian), the other 2 to 1.
- **Every interval is a consonance**: unison, 3rd, 5th, 6th, octave and their compounds. 2nds, 4ths, 7ths and the tritone are dissonant and not allowed in first species.
- **Imperfect consonances** (3rds, 6ths) may be approached any way; **perfect consonances** (unison, 5th, octave) only by **contrary motion**, to avoid direct fifths and octaves.
- Not more than **three 3rds** (or **6ths**) in a row.
- When the cantus firmus is in the upper part, the counterpoint below uses unison, 3rd, 5th or 6th.
- Only these **leaps**: 3rds, 4ths, 5ths, ascending minor 6ths, octaves; after a leap larger than a 4th, change direction. Do not outline a tritone with two turning points. Avoid repeated notes (they hold up the flow).

## 30.3 Second species: two against one

Write **two half notes** against each whole note of the cantus firmus. (In 3/2, three half notes against a dotted whole.) The rules are the same on the downbeats, with these changes:

- **Begin** with a half note at the octave or unison on beat 1, or on beat 3 after a half rest.
- **End** with a whole note on the octave or unison. The bar before: with the cantus firmus below, a **5th then a 6th** above it (6 7 against the cantus firmus's 2); with it above, a **5th then a 3rd** below it. (Phrygian, cantus firmus above: a 6th then a 3rd.)
- The first half note of a bar is always a consonance. The second is a consonance, **or a dissonance only as a passing tone** (reached and left by step in the same direction).
- Across the barline, imperfect consonances are free, perfect ones only by contrary motion. **Do not repeat a note across a barline.** Avoid octaves on consecutive downbeats, and fifths on consecutive downbeats, unless a leap of a 4th follows the first.

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="2" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 G3 E3 D3" data-cp='[[null,"D4"],["B3","G3"],["B3","C#4"],["D4"]]' data-expect="ok">A four-bar example: half rest then D (octave), a bar of 3rd and unison, the 5th to 6th before the end, the final octave.</div>

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="2" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 G3 E3 D3" data-cp='[[null,"D4"],["B3","A3"],["B3","C#4"],["D4"]]' data-expect="passing">Bar 2: the A over G is a dissonant second half note that is left by a leap, not a passing tone.</div>

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="2" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 G3 E3 D3" data-cp='[[null,"D4"],["B3","B3"],["B3","C#4"],["D4"]]' data-expect="repeat">Bar 2 ends on B and bar 3 begins on B: a repeated note across the barline.</div>

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="2" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 G3 E3 D3" data-cp='[[null,"D4"],["B3","G3"],["G3","B3"],["D4"]]' data-expect="bar before the end">The bar before the end is a 3rd and a 5th, not the 5th and 6th the ending needs.</div>


### Exercise: second species

**Cantus firmus below** (D dorian). Begin with a half rest and a half note `D4` (leave the first box of bar 1 empty). Bar 5 is the bar before the end: a fifth and a sixth above E3. The last bar is one box.

<div class="vl-species" data-species="2" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 F3 G3 F3 E3 D3" data-hint="Two boxes a bar; the last bar one. Second notes that are dissonant must be passing tones."></div>


## 30.4 Third, fourth and fifth species

- **Third species**: four quarter notes to a whole note; each downbeat a consonance; passing tones allowed (never on the downbeat) and the **cambiata**; the penultimate bar uses set formulas.
- **Fourth species**: **suspensions** and syncopations. The half note on beat 3 is tied over the barline; if it is a dissonance (4th or 7th) it is a suspension and must resolve down by step (4-3 and 7-6 are allowed in the upper part, 9-8 and 2-1 are not); the penultimate bar has a 7-6 suspension. In the book the cantus firmus is in the lower voice.
- **Fifth species** (florid counterpoint) is a free mix of all the others.

*These are not checked by this page's checker.*

## 30.5 Invention expositions and fugue analysis

The chapter ends with applying species to harmony: writing the four-bar **exposition** of a two-part invention on the model of Bach's C major and E minor inventions (the theme in bar 1, an octave lower in the bass in bar 2, a fifth higher in bar 3, an octave lower in bar 4, ending on a tenth: tonic in the bass, 3 above), with counterpoint that outlines the harmony of each bar
(I, then V, then back to I); and **analysing a fugue**: subject, answer (real or tonal), countersubject, episode, bridge and exposition, with motivic fragmentation. Open the Bach
fugue and invention scores in the [Analysed Scores Library](analysed-scores/view.qmd) to hear and see them. *Not checked here.*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the checker does and does not check
- First species: beginning, ending (contrary, 7 to 8 and 2 to 1), consonance, perfect intervals only by contrary motion, runs of 3rds and 6ths (this site reads it as three of the same kind), allowed leaps, direction change after leaps larger than a 4th, outlined tritones, repeated notes (a warning).
- Second species: the beginning on beat 1 or 3, the whole-note ending, the penultimate-bar formulas, consonant downbeats, dissonant second notes only as passing tones, no repeated note across the barline, no octaves or fifths on consecutive downbeats unless a 4th leap follows.
- **Not checked:** consecutive leaps outlining a triad in species, the range of the counterpoint, and everything in 30.4 and 30.5.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
